lessons.title: Prohibited practices (Article 5)
lessons.subtitle: Eight AI practices prohibited in the EU since 2 February 2025
keyConcepts: Fine of up to 7% of annual turnover

sections.title: The risk-based approach and the off switch
sections.content:
The AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) has four levels: unacceptable risk with eight prohibited practices (**Article 5**), high risk (Article 6 in conjunction with Annexes I and III), limited risk with a transparency duty (Article 50) and the minimal-risk remainder.

Only Article 5 has no compliance path: if a system matches one of the eight prohibited patterns, it has to go. Placing on the market, putting into service and use are prohibited (Article 5(1)) since **2 February 2025** (Article 113, point (a)), with no transition period and no SME exemption.

Fines reach the Regulation's highest tier, **up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover**, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)).

The Commission's **Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices** of 4 February 2025 interpret points (a) to (h).

sections.title: The eight prohibited practices in Article 5(1), points (a) to (h)
sections.content:
Article 5(1) lists eight categories exhaustively. Points (f) and (g) hit SMEs most often.

- **Point (a):** manipulative or subliminal techniques that cause significant harm, such as a dark-pattern bot that talks consumers into insurance.
- **Point (b):** exploiting vulnerability due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, such as AI marketing that targets people in debt with credit offers.
- **Point (c):** social scoring with detrimental treatment in an unrelated context, such as a supplier score that links the managing directors' social-media activity to payment terms.
- **Point (d):** predictive policing based solely on profiling.
- **Point (e):** untargeted scraping of facial images to build databases (the Clearview AI prohibition).
- **Point (f):** emotion recognition in the workplace and in education institutions, except for medical or safety reasons. Software that reads facial expressions or personality in interview videos has been prohibited since February 2025, even if vendors still advertise it in 2026.
- **Point (g):** biometric categorisation by race, political opinion, religion, trade-union membership or sex life.
- **Point (h):** real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces, with narrow exceptions for law enforcement (Article 5(2) to (7), Annex II).

sections.title: What an SME has to check
sections.content:
**If a tool measures emotions, biometrics or social behaviour and attaches consequences to the result, check it against Article 5.** Typical cases:

- A plastics manufacturer wants to spot stress in machine operators by webcam to optimise shifts: prohibited under point (f).
- An insurer scores applicants on public social-media posts: prohibited under point (c) once the detrimental treatment is unrelated to the context.

Also check every tool for steering decisions, and allow 30 to 60 minutes per system. Consent from the people affected or approval from the works council does not cure an Article 5 infringement. The Federal Network Agency's AI Service Desk has given free initial information since July 2025.

If you find such a tool, stop using it and get legal advice.

quiz.questionText: A plastics manufacturer with 120 employees wants webcams to detect stressed machine operators and optimise shifts. Is this permitted?

answerOptions.text: Yes, because it is used only for shift planning
Yes, with employee and works council consent
No, Article 5(1), point (f), prohibits workplace emotion recognition
Yes, provided the data is processed only internally

quiz.explanation: Article 5(1), point (f), prohibits workplace emotion recognition, and consent or a works council does not cure it. Only medical or safety purposes, such as fatigue detection in professional drivers, are exempt.

quiz.questionText: What is the maximum fine for an infringement of Article 5?

answerOptions.text: Up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% of turnover
Up to EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover
Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover
Up to EUR 50 million or 10% of turnover

quiz.explanation: Article 99(3) sets the highest tier for Article 5 infringements; the obligations in Article 99(4) sit lower at EUR 15 million or 3%.

quiz.questionText: An insurer scores applicants on public social-media posts and treats them worse without any link to the insurance line. Which practice is this?

answerOptions.text: A high-risk system under Annex III, point 5
Prohibited social scoring under Article 5(1), point (c)
Limited risk with a transparency obligation under Article 50
Minimal risk because the social-media data is public

quiz.explanation: Article 5(1), point (c), prohibits scoring by social behaviour that leads to detrimental treatment in an unrelated context. Public availability of the data changes nothing.

lessons.title: High risk: Annex I and Annex III
lessons.subtitle: Two routes into the high-risk class and one exception

sections.title: Route 1: a safety component of a regulated product under Article 6(1)
sections.content:
AI in a lift control is high-risk through **Annex I**, the first route into the high-risk class. It lists around 20 EU harmonisation acts, among them Machinery Regulation 2023/1230, Medical Devices Regulation 2017/745, IVDR 2017/746, Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC, Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU, Lifts Directive 2014/33/EU, motor-vehicle type approval, aviation (EASA), rail and marine equipment.

Under **Article 6(1)** an AI system is high-risk where it is the safety component of an Annex I product or is itself such a product, **and** the sectoral act requires a third-party conformity assessment. Examples are an AI module in a plant control with a protective shutdown (Machinery Regulation) and a medical AI device (Medical Devices Regulation).

Legal consequence: the sectoral conformity assessment **plus** the obligations in Articles 8 to 15, covered in block 3.

sections.title: Route 2: stand-alone high-risk systems under Article 6(2) and the eight Annex III areas
sections.content:
Under **Article 6(2)**, independent of paragraph 1, an AI system is high-risk where it is used in one of the **eight Annex III areas**. Paragraph 3 holds a narrow counter-exception for pure support functions.

1. **Biometrics:** remote identification, categorisation by sensitive attributes, emotion recognition where Article 5 does not prohibit it.
2. **Critical infrastructure:** AI as a safety component in digital infrastructure, road traffic, water, gas, heating and electricity, for example at municipal utilities.
3. **Education and vocational training:** admission and assessment AI, exam monitoring, for example exam software at vocational schools.
4. **Employment and HR:** recruitment, **CV screening** and candidate evaluation (point 4(a)), plus promotion, termination, task allocation and performance monitoring (point 4(b)). CV ranking in an applicant-tracking system can fall under point 4(a); the intended purpose decides.
5. **Essential services:** public assistance, creditworthiness assessment and credit scoring, life and health insurance pricing, emergency-call prioritisation, for example at insurance brokers.
6. **Law enforcement** and 7. **migration, asylum, border control:** public-authority territory, rarely relevant to an SME.
8. **Justice and democratic processes:** assistants to research and interpret facts and law (Annex III, point 8(a)), AI intended to influence elections (point 8(b)).

Providers meet Article 16 and the requirements in Articles 9 to 15 (block 3), deployers Article 26. The fundamental rights impact assessment in Article 27 binds only the addressees named there. The rules apply from **2 December 2027** for stand-alone Annex III systems and from **2 August 2028** for product-embedded systems (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026).

sections.title: The exception in Article 6(3)
sections.content:
Under **Article 6(3)** a system used in an Annex III area is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision-making. That can apply where the AI system:

- **(a)** performs a narrow procedural task;
- **(b)** improves the result of a completed human activity;
- **(c)** detects decision patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the completed human assessment without proper human review; or
- **(d)** performs a preparatory task for an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case.

**Profiling rules the exception out.** Whoever relies on it documents the assessment under Article 6(4) and registers the system in the EU database under Article 49(2).

Market surveillance may check at any time whether the exception applies. If an applicant-tracking vendor takes its pre-sorting module out of the high-risk class this way, the **deployer** still checks the classification; trust it blindly and you answer for the misjudgement.

quiz.questionText: Personio's AI Performance Summaries condense 360-degree feedback before the manager reads it. How is this use classified?

answerOptions.text: Limited risk, because it only summarises
High risk under Article 6(2) in conjunction with Annex III, point 4(b)
Minimal risk because a human makes the final decision
A prohibited practice under Article 5(1), point (c)

quiz.explanation: Annex III, point 4(b), covers AI for performance evaluation. Choosing what stands out shapes the evaluation, even if a human decides.

quiz.questionText: Which system is high-risk through Article 6(1) and Annex I, not Annex III?

answerOptions.text: AI as a safety component of a lift control (Directive 2014/33/EU)
An applicant-management system with ranking
Credit scoring at a cooperative bank
Exam-monitoring AI at a vocational school

quiz.explanation: The lift control is a safety component of an Annex I product (Article 6(1)); the other three cases are in Annex III.

quiz.questionText: What must a provider do when it uses Article 6(3) to keep an Annex III system out of the high-risk class?

answerOptions.text: Nothing needs documenting
Document the assessment (Article 6(4)) and register the system (Article 49(2))
Nothing, the system is exempt from every AI Act obligation
Use profiling, as long as it is preparatory

quiz.explanation: The assessment must be documented (Article 6(4)) and the system registered (Article 49(2)); profiling rules out the exception.

lessons.title: Limited risk: transparency under Article 50
lessons.subtitle: Disclosure duties for chatbots and AI content from 2 August 2026

sections.title: Who is responsible, and from when
sections.content:
From **2 August 2026** (Article 113, point (c)), Article 50 binds **providers** (paragraphs 1 and 2), who build the system, and **deployers** (paragraphs 3 and 4), who use it in their own organisation. Recital 132 gives the reason: people need to know when they are talking to a machine or looking at artificial content.

Infringements cost **up to EUR 15 million or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover**, whichever is higher (Article 99(4), point (g)).

sections.title: The four transparency cases
sections.content:
Article 50 has four cases:

- **Paragraph 1, AI interaction:** providers design systems for direct interaction so that people recognise they are interacting with AI. Exceptions cover obvious cases and, under narrow conditions, law enforcement.
- **Paragraph 2, synthetic content:** providers of generative systems for audio, image, video or text mark covered outputs in **machine-readable** form. The solution has to be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible and in line with the state of the art; the Regulation prescribes no single technology.
- **Paragraph 3, emotion recognition and biometric categorisation:** deployers inform the people affected, where Article 5 permits the system at all.
- **Paragraph 4, deepfakes and AI text:** deployers disclose deepfakes visibly, in an adapted form for artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works. AI-generated text on matters of public interest has to be disclosed unless a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility. A synthetic product photo is not automatically a deepfake.

sections.title: What limited risk does not mean
sections.content:
Article 50 demands **no** high-risk duties such as a risk-management system, technical documentation or conformity assessment, only visible or machine-readable disclosure.

If a system is also high-risk, Article 50 still applies. An HR chatbot that screens applicants needs the notice under Article 50(1) **and** risk management, logging and human oversight under Article 6(2) in conjunction with Annex III, point 4.

Platforms on which the content appears fall under separate Digital Services Act rules. The disclosure belongs where the person meets the content; a blanket footer notice is not enough.

sections.title: Your rights as an AI user
sections.content:
From 2 August 2026 you have to be told before or at the first interaction that you are dealing with AI, unless that is obvious anyway (Article 50(1)).

The voluntary **Code of Practice on transparency** of 10 June 2026 supports the implementation of Article 50(2), (4) and (5). It is a compliance aid, does not replace the statutory text and is no automatic proof of conformity.

**What you can do:**

1. **Report:** send suspicious or misleading content through the platform's reporting channel.
2. **Check:** origin, context and original source. Detection tools give indications, not proof of authenticity.
3. **Complain:** Article 85 provides for complaints to the competent market-surveillance authority. Germany's KI-MIG entered into force on 29 July 2026 and makes the Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur) the market-surveillance authority, single point of contact and complaints office, as far as no specialised authority is competent. Use the currently published filing routes.

(Source: Articles 50 and 85 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; European Commission, Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content, 10 June 2026; German Bundestag decision on the KI-MIG, 11 June 2026)
sections.keyTakeaway: The role-based duties in Article 50 apply from 2 August 2026. Technical marking (providers, paragraph 2) and visible deepfake disclosure (deployers, paragraph 4) are separate duties.

quiz.questionText: A print company's marketing team publishes blog articles that an AI writes alone. Nobody edits them. Which obligation applies?

answerOptions.text: None, provided the content is accurate
A general footer notice that the company uses AI
Visible disclosure on each article under Article 50(4), second subparagraph
Registration of the AI system in the EU database under Article 49

quiz.explanation: Article 50(4), second subparagraph, requires visible disclosure on the text itself where nobody holds editorial responsibility.

quiz.questionText: A chatbot on a construction firm's careers page answers applicant questions and pre-sorts CVs by experience. Which regime applies?

answerOptions.text: Only Article 50(1), the AI-interaction notice
Only Article 6(2) with Annex III, point 4
Both: Article 50(1) and Annex III, point 4(a)
Neither, because it only pre-sorts

quiz.explanation: The risk classes are not mutually exclusive. Pre-sorting is an Annex III function, so the firm needs risk management, logging and human oversight on top of the chatbot notice.

quiz.questionText: Who is responsible for deepfake disclosure under Article 50(4)?

answerOptions.text: The provider of the AI model, such as OpenAI
The deployer that discloses the deepfake to the public
The platform on which the deepfake appears
The photographer who created the original image

quiz.explanation: Article 50(4) addresses the deployer that uses and publishes the deepfake. Providers mark outputs machine-readably under paragraph 2, and platforms fall under the Digital Services Act.

lessons.title: Minimal risk and the decision tree
lessons.subtitle: How six questions settle the risk class
keyConcepts: Minimal risk as the residual category

sections.title: What minimal risk means in practice
sections.content:
**Minimal risk** is the remainder and the largest class in an SME: everything that falls neither under Article 5, nor under Article 6 (Annex I or III), nor under Article 50. Typical examples:

- ChatGPT for internal email drafts
- DeepL for translations with no personal data
- quality-control image recognition on the production line with no personal data
- spam filtering on the mail server
- predictive maintenance on machine data
- route planning, warehouse management
- GitHub Copilot for code completion

There are no risk-class-specific AI Act duties here, but **Article 4 on AI literacy** applies to every class, and Article 95 encourages voluntary codes of conduct. The tools are still AI systems under Article 3(1).

sections.title: The decision tree in six questions
sections.content:
Work through these questions in order, per use case rather than per tool:

1. **Is it an AI system under Article 3(1)**, a machine-based system with a degree of autonomy that generates predictions, recommendations or decisions? If not, as with a hard-coded Excel formula, the AI Act does not apply.
2. **Does it fall under the prohibitions in Article 5(1)?** If yes, switch it off or rebuild it.
3. **Is it a safety component under Annex I (Article 6(1))?** If yes, high risk: sectoral conformity assessment plus Articles 8 to 15.
4. **Does it influence a decision in one of the eight Annex III areas (Article 6(2))?** If yes, high risk: Articles 8 to 15 plus Article 26 and, for the deployers named there, Article 27. Examine and document the exception in Article 6(3).
5. **Does one of the four Article 50 cases apply** (chatbot, synthetic content, emotion or biometrics, deepfake or AI text with no editorial responsibility)? If yes, limited risk with a transparency duty.
6. **All no:** minimal risk, with Article 4 and voluntary codes of conduct under Article 95.

ChatGPT for a meeting summary is minimal risk; ChatGPT for pre-sorting applications falls under Annex III, point 4, and is high-risk.

sections.title: The asymmetry of misclassification
sections.content:
**Too low** (high risk treated as minimal): risk management, logging or human oversight can be missing. Once the duties apply, market-surveillance measures and penalties under Article 99 come into play; parallel law such as the General Equal Treatment Act or the GDPR can bite earlier.

**Too high** (minimal treated as high risk): unnecessary compliance work, system by system.

Document the purpose, the role and the Article 6 assessment against the annexes. If a legal question stays open, write it down and set a risk-appropriate interim control. Do not wait for 2 December 2027.

**Apply it now:** work through the six questions for your most important AI system and enter the risk class and reasoning in your AI inventory (risk-classification column).

quiz.questionText: A tax adviser uses DATEV's AI receipt capture to read invoice amounts and assign accounts. What is the risk profile?

answerOptions.text: Prohibited under Article 5 (profiling)
High risk under Annex III, point 5 (creditworthiness)
Minimal risk: no decision about people, no Annex III, no Article 50
Limited risk, because the assignment is automated

quiz.explanation: Receipt capture meets no case under Article 5, 6 or 50 and is minimal risk; Article 4 still applies.

quiz.questionText: Which obligation still applies to minimal-risk AI use?

answerOptions.text: Human oversight under Article 14
AI literacy under Article 4
Transparency obligations under Article 50
A fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27

quiz.explanation: Article 4 has applied to every risk class since 2 February 2025; Articles 14, 50 and 27 apply only to high risk, transparency cases or specific deployers.

quiz.questionText: An IT service firm with 40 employees uses ChatGPT for (a) meeting summaries, (b) email drafts and (c) pre-selecting freelancer profiles. How is each use classified?

answerOptions.text: All three minimal, because it is the same tool
(a) and (b) minimal, (c) high-risk under Annex III, point 4(a)
All three high-risk, because ChatGPT is a general-purpose AI model
All three limited risk, because Article 50 always applies to ChatGPT

quiz.explanation: Classification runs per use case: pre-selecting freelancers filters candidates for work (Annex III, point 4(a)); summaries and emails do not.

props.title: The risk pyramid in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
props.caption: Play the sequence from the strictest level at the top (prohibited) to the freest at the bottom (minimal).

props.title: Order the four risk levels
props.prompt: Sort the four risk classes from the deepest intervention at the top to the lowest at the bottom. Drag the cards or use the arrow buttons.
props.hint: First question: is it prohibited? Then: high-risk? Then: does a transparency duty apply? What is left over is minimal risk.
